speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: TABLING OF ORDER IN COUNCIL RESPECTING BENEFITS TO MARRIED WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave of the house to table copies of order in council P.C. 1957-1477 revoking section 161 of the regulations of the Unemployment Insurance Act regarding married women. Perhaps for the information of the house I might make a statement at this time.
I should like to announce that effective November 17 the unemployment insurance commission is revoking its regulation that imposed additional conditions for the receipt of unemployment insurance benefit on certain married women. In other words, as far as unemployment insurance is concerned married women in the labour force will now be on exactly the same footing as all other claimants in the labour force.
Perhaps I should take a minute or two in order to outline the events and reasonings that led to this decision, and I believe I can best begin by noting the special conditions to which married women have been subject.
In effect, the regulation required any woman who claimed benefit within two years after the date of her marriage to have 10 contribution weeks during that period; and further, if she was working at the time of her marriage the 10 contribution weeks had to be made after her first separation from that employment. This special condition purported to show that the claimant had not left the labour market as a consequence of getting married.
There were, of course, exceptions to this rule. The additional condition did not have to be fulfilled if her separation from employment was a consequence of her employer's policy against retaining married women; or if, for instance, she was laid off because of a shortage of work. But in spite of the exceptions quite a number of married women have been affected by this regulation ever since it came into being.
The married women's regulation was introduced in 1950, and it has had a stormy life in the seven years of its existence. As with everything that has overtones of discrimination, it has been a focal point for controversy, and that is perhaps one of the most cogent reasons for abandoning it.
At the time this regulation was introduced it was argued that a goodly number of newly married women, who had ceased to depend entirely on their own earnings, were nevertheless representing themselves as seeking work for the purpose of drawing benefit. I have always felt that this was a highly dangerous argument since it implied that one knew, without possibility of error, what was in another person's mind.
Again, it was suggested that married women were making far more claims in proportion to their numbers than were single women or men. This again was a dangerous argument, since it involved casting the shadow of suspicion on an entire class numbering in the hundreds of thousands because it was felt, although it could not be proved, that there was chicanery on the part of a few.
Since 1950 I know various hon. members have from time to time fulminated against the provisions of this regulation. Perhaps the most persistent and effective champion of the rights of married women in this regard is the Secretary of State, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). Again, throughout the recent election campaign the Conservative party promised that one of their first acts in office would be the revocation of this regulation.
I think there are two basic reasons why we rejected the arguments of those who were its proponents. First, there is an almost natural repugnance against anything that has the slightest shading of discrimination, even though the motives of those who favour it are of the highest. Second, and perhaps more important, I believe we sensed that those who favoured the married women's regulations were completely ignoring one inexorable fact. That fact was that the working wife or mother was not a temporary product of world war II but was in fact the indication of a new social trend. If married women in the labour force had only been a temporary phenomenon of the war years and the immediate post-war years, in all likelihood this particular problem would long ago have solved itself. But the married woman in the labour force has long since proved herself to be no temporary phenomenon.
From June 1951 to June 1957 the number of married women in the labour force increased from 303,000 to 543,000, a gain of 80 per cent. Some of this increase is due no doubt to older women returning to employment when their children have reached an age when they no longer require their
1172	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance mother's full time. It is, however, probably safe to assume that the increase is due in the main to the growing extent to which single women, upon becoming married, continue to work. This I think is the new social trend which I noted a few moments ago.
Because of the economic factors that have been at work during these past years more and more women have found it necessary to continue working after marriage in order to maintain a reasonable standard of living. Again, it is likely that many married women continue to work because they enjoy the stimulation of the many contacts afforded by a working day as opposed to the housewifely routine. It is a known fact that nowadays many women take a temporary leave of absence for the purpose of childbirth and resume their normal working routine as soon as satisfactory arrangements are made for the care of the child. This is a pattern that has now won wide acceptance both in industry and in the civil service. And, I might add, it is a pattern that strongly indicates that married women are in the labour force to stay, for as far into the future as one can look.
In view of the undoubted importance and permanence of married women as working women, there is no justification for retaining a regulation which implies that statements made by them as to availability and willingness to work are less reliable than similar statements made by other classes of insured persons. There is no justification for retaining a regulation that forces married women to be treated differently from other groups, such as persons who are on pension from their former employers and seasonal workers. Most of all there is no justification for retaining a regulation that discriminates against those married women who, although unable to meet the additional condition that applies to them, are genuinely in the labour market.
I believe that whatever good it may have done is far outweighed by this single effect it has had.
I should like to conclude by noting that each year some 12,000 married women will now be entitled to the protection of unemployment insurance benefit, protection that this regulation has prevented them from receiving. By that I mean 12,000 is the number of married women who were disqualified in the past year by regulation 161. Although this revocation is not retroactive, I would suggest that married women who have been disqualified under this regulation should get in touch with their national employment office to have their claims reviewed. In the event that the review of their claim indicates that the disqualification might be removed, we would wish to have no delay in the implementation of that removal.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    STATEMENT ON EXPLOSIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN AND MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several hon. members have asked questions in regard to the result of the investigation into the breaks on the Trans-Canada pipe line, and I have now a report from the board of transport commissioners to the effect that:
All of the breaks experienced in our testing program so far have occurred because of a fatigue crack in the parent metal of the pipe, but we have not determined what causes this fatigue nor what limits it to a relatively short length, 2 inches to 18 inches, along the factory weld in the pipe. The pressure within the pipe finally overstresses the remaining metal and the rapid propagation of the pressure wave brought about by that failure results in a tearing and ripping action in the metal itself.
While there has been no determination as to the cause, the board of transport commissioners are advised that the Battelle Memorial Institute, an independent research laboratory, has been hired to make an investigation into the cause of the failure, and the board has not yet received from the company the results of its investigation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 30 the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) asked me the following question:
Has the minister's attention been drawn to the statement of Mr. A. Beasley, chief of the View Royal fire brigade, appearing in the Victoria Daily Colonist of October 23 in connection with the recent fire on the Songhees reserve which cost the lives of two Indian children, in which Mr. Beasley stated that the Indian affairs branch carries out no inspection of chimneys and other fire hazards on the reserve and that the Indian agent at Duncan had failed to reply to four letters written by Mr. Beasley in regard to fire protection on the reserve?
If so, can the minister inform the house as to the correctness of Mr. Beasley's assertion that no inspection is carried out, and can he tell the house whether his department is considering entering into agreements with municipalities contiguous to Indian reserves to ensure fire protection on the reserves?
I want to apologize to the hon. member for the length of time which has elapsed between his question and my reply, but I wanted to get the facts absolutely correctly. I have now received a report from the superintendent of the Cowichan Indian agency in which the Songhees reserve is located, and in which he advises that the fire occurred in a large old building occupied by Mrs. Thomas George at 1441 Craig-flower road. Mrs. George was caring for six grandchildren. It is thought that fire started in the stovepipe connecting a cook stove and the chimney. The outbreak was seen by passers-by on the well-travelled highway which passes the house, and four children were brought out of the house with the grandmother. Unfortunately two could not be found in the smoke, and were burned to death. The report continues that the superintendent of the agency went to Victoria immediately and helped the chief make arrangements for rehabilitation of the family, and he wishes to go on record as saying that the chief and council did an excellent job of


organizing, and the generosity of friends and neighbours, both Indian and white, was overwhelming.
Now with regard to the allegations in the newspapers, in the Victoria Times on Wednesday evening, October 23, there was a leading article which stated in part as follows:
Chief Beasley criticized the department of Indian affairs for not sending agents to inspect chimneys in the Songhees Indian reserve.
Although not responsible for the area the brigade answered the alarm as a courtesy, he said.
Recently he wrote four letters to the Indian agent at Duncan complaining about the lack of fire inspection.
Chief Beasley claimed he didn't even have the courtesy to reply.
The agency superintendent reports that he interviewed Mr. Beasley that same evening, asking him to produce copies of the letters he alleged had been sent. Chief Beasley claimed that the reporter had made a mistake and denied that he had ever sent as many as four letters, but he maintained that about seven months ago he had written a letter to that office.
The superintendent advises further that on his return to the agency next day he made a careful search of their filing system but could find no trace of any letter from Mr. Beasley, nor could any member of his staff recollect having seen such a letter.
The superintendent has since written to Mr. Beasley asking him for a copy of this letter in order that he might know exactly what was proposed. The superintendent adds that, during the conversation referred to, he asked Mr. Beasley if his fire department would be interested in negotiating an agreement to provide fire protection to the Songhees and Esquimalt reserves, such as are in existence with other fire departments in that agency. Chief Beasley said he would take it up with the officers of the View Royal fire department and let the superintendent know. This conversation has been confirmed in writing by the superintendent, but as at the date of his report he had received no reply.
In answer to the other part of the question with regard to this matter, since 1955 it has been and still is the policy of the department to negotiate, wherever possible, agreements with municipalities for the extension of fire protection to reserves adjacent to municipalities. It appears that no such agreement has been negotiated for this particular reserve, but that matter is under negotiation at the present time.

A few days before the election of June 10 two men, Charles Kratzmeir and Ambrose Truman, were hired by the Department of Public Works purely on a party basis and neglecting any question of veterans preference. On election day they took part in the election in support of the former government. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is to be any budget, which of course I doubt very much, and if there is to be any decrease in taxes, I hope that with regard to income tax the government will respect the family organization of agriculture in the province of Quebec, and will not impose unwonted charges on a system of agriculture which has been the strength of our nation.
I hope the basic exemptions with regard to income tax will be increased from $1,000 to $1,500 for single persons and from $2,000 to $3,000 for married taxpayers, in line with the wish I have expressed more than once on the floor of the house and also in line with promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Let us hope, too, that the Unemployment Insurance Act will be amended to take into account agricultural problems and, more particularly, to cover agricultural workers. I also hope the qualifying period for unemployment insurance will be reduced.
I take advantage of this opportunity to protest against the new trade policy of the government. The London government knows full well that Canada is incapable of allowing British industry free access to our markets. This would spell the doom of our woollen and
The Address-Mr. LaCroix cotton mills, of our factories producing shoes, gloves, slippers and other goods, which provide employment to several hundred thousand workers in Canada, several hundred of whom are in my own constituency. At the present time these industries survive only because of the protection afforded by customs tariffs. Free trade, preferential tariffs or anything of the sort would certainly bring about their disappearance. Everyone knows that the cost price of anything made in England is lower than that of goods manufactured in this country, where salaries are higher.
The attitude adopted by the Conservative government since it has come into power with regard to our trade relations with Great Britain has caused unemployment in almost every branch of industry and commerce in this country. At the present time there is unemployment on a scale unknown since the days of the Bennett administration. Mr. Bennett had already tried his economic policies with England, and the only thing they brought our country was a period of intense unemployment and, to Mr. Bennett, a seat in the British House of Lords where he spent the rest of his life. Unless we maintain the Liberal policy of protecting our industries against depreciated currency and low salary countries our Canadian industries will be wiped out and foreign investments in this country will diminish. The best means to increase our exports to the United States is to insist upon the processing of our natural resources here in Canada, as we have already done in the case of pulpwood and as we should do also in the case of iron ore, processing the latter into steel by means of smelters built in Canada. That would facilitate shipping through the St. Lawrence seaway and reduce our trade deficit with the United States.
Representatives of several manufacturing concerns in several industrial sectors have already stated categorically that to accept the British proposal or something similar would be deliberately courting disaster. It would mean the shutting down of several factories and the laying off of many thousands of Canadian workers at a time when owing to a recession in a certain sphere of our economy and to wide scale immigration, unemployment is on the increase. As a result of the high salaries and the standard of living prevailing in this country, in many fields we cannot compete with British industry and the industries of many commonwealth countries. This new trend which is apparently taking place in the trade policy of Canada will likely cause another period of uncertainty in financial circles, which will then hesitate to make further industrial investments as long as the future trends of our trade policy are not definitely set out.

The Address-Mr. LaCroix The Prime Minister, who before the election of last June 10 blamed the Liberal government for not standing by England's side in her declaration of war on Egypt, notwithstanding the fact that Great Britain had not consulted Canada, went through his whole electoral campaign stirring up the fanatical feelings of certain imperialists in Canada on this subject. However, the day after the election he did not hesitate to put under the direction of an American the whole of our air defence thus sacrificing our independence; and he did so after a conference with the United States Secretary of State, at which he had meant to speak firmly to the Americans. The only result so far discernible by Canadians is that the Prime Minister of their country has beaten a hasty retreat.
Since the last British garrison left our shores, about a century ago, we have assumed full authority over our armed forces. By this fact Canada has been able at least to direct its own international policy, of which military establishments are but an expression. It is owing to this Canadian independence in military matters that the hon. member for Prince Albert, acting as leader of the opposition, could blame the Canadian government last year for following the policy of the United States in the Suez incident instead of pursuing a policy which should have been, in his opinion, an endorsement of the British operation. That, however, would not only have brought us automatically in the war beside England, but would have unmistakably brought on a third world war, which fortunately we were spared thanks to the firm attitude of Canada's former secretary of state for external affairs, the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), whose gallant efforts in that field have just earned him the award of the Nobel prize for peace, a unique honour since he is the first Canadian to receive this prize for his contribution to world peace. How will Canada be in a position to pursue its own foreign policy if national defence passes to United States command?
I wish to draw another matter to the attention of the government. Here are the comments made by L' Action Catholique on Tuesday, September 10, 1957, after Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had announced his decision to relinquish the Liberal party leadership:
History will recognize that the Hon. Mr. St. Laurent was a great prime minister. At all times, he has enjoyed the respect and consideration of all Canadians. He had political opponents taut no enemy.
Notwithstanding certain attitudes which they would have liked to be different, French Canadians will admit that, under the administration of the Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, the cause of bilingualism in Canada and of our representation in the civil service has improved. His views and actions in

such matters have placed his successors in a position from which they cannot back out with impunity.
Has our racial group lost ground since June 10 last as far as its representation and influence are concerned? The following is what I read on that subject in Le Soleil of Friday, August 9, 1957:
It will be the first time in a very long time that the French element is reduced to such a minor role in the administration of our country, which is bad from the simple electoral point of view for the party in power and particularly for Canadian politics.
With two ministers confined to minor assignments the voice of French Canada will hardly be heard. Such a situation is a matter of concern not only for the province of Quebec but for all political observers who have the future of our country at heart. Looking back on history, Mr. Bruce Hutchison, in a recent issue of the Financial Post, said that the first condition of success for a Canadian government was to rely on the support of French and English Canada.
As for the criticisms levelled at the government on that score, the new Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) said in Montreal that the province of Quebec must elect more Conservative members if it wants more representatives in the Progressive Conservative government. He also emphasized the fact that his leader had chosen three ministers among the eight Conservative members elected in Quebec. He even felt it necessary to add that those three ministers hold very important posts.
The Prime Minister was in the position of a lawyer who must rely on doubtful arguments to defend a very bad case. British Columbia has three representatives in the cabinet, including the Minister of Justice, (Mr. Fulton), and these three departments are still more important than the three assigned to Quebec representatives. Yet British Columbia elected but seven Conservative members, and its population is but one-third of Quebec's population.
It is possible, without violating parliamentary tradition, to choose ministers outside the House of Commons. The Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, did not hesitate to call on Mr. Sidney Smith of the University of Toronto to make him his Secretary of State for External Affairs. French Canadians, on the other hand, must be satisfied with two ministers, since the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton), the third Quebec minister, represents the Anglo-protestant minority, and those two representatives must accept the two least important portfolios of the whole federal administration.
The appointment of the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave the province of Ontario a seventh representative in the cabinet. However, in a speech delivered on television some time after the election the

Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) told us that the eight elected Conservative members in Quebec were all qualified for ministerial positions, a statement confirmed recently by the Prime Minister in a television broadcast. The Prime Minister argued that we are living in a bilingual country. I can tell him, in this respect, that it is not enough to come to the province of Quebec and read a few words, with the help of a Mona Lisa smile, to convince my fellow citizens of his sincerity, but it is necessary to translate those ideas into facts.

Otherwise the voters of
Quebec might take the liberty in 1958 to show the Prime Minister, who calls the tune and attempts to follow the devious and brutal policy of give and take, that Quebec is more than an ordinary province. This it will do by making him feel deeply sorry for playing this little game of hide and seek, even if he keeps playing it until the very eve of the next election.
I would like to avail myself of the opportunity offered by this debate, Mr. Speaker, to ask the government, as I have done on previous occasions for at least 20 years, for a distinctive Canadian flag. There is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that the government will agree to solve this Canadian flag problem which has been plaguing us ever since confederation and which, as long as it remains unsolved, will maintain our country in a ridiculous position in the eyes of the world. Yet a solution would be welcome, the matter being more than ever topical.
The time seems ripe for action, Mr. Speaker. Our fellow citizens throughout the country appear ready to make certain concessions. The Toronto Star cited a few interesting facts in this connection the other day. For example, the Toronto junior chamber of commerce adopted a resolution indicating in no uncertain terms its wish for the adoption of a national flag containing neither the fleur-de-lis nor the union jack. For a protestant and English-speaking group to have adopted such a resolution without this giving rise to acrimonious debate among its members is certainly proof that the fanaticism of certain people is on the wane. The Toronto Star also indicates that a similar resolution has been adopted by the Toronto section of the native sons of Canada.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I have prepared an amendment which in every shape and form I would consider to be not a nonconfidence motion.
The Address-Mr. LaCroix
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pontiac-Timiskaming (Mr. Proudfoot), that the following be added to the address:
We respectfully urge, however, that Canada should have a distinctive national flag and, in the opinion of this house, Your Most Gracious Majesty's advisers should consider at once the advisability of taking steps to give to this country a truly Canadian flag.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a pleasure not unmixed with emotion that I now rise to speak on behalf of the constituency of Kamouraska. The atmosphere of dignity which befits this house never fails to impress a new member, but the sympathetic welcome of the hon. members, regardless of the party they belong to, is comforting to the newly elected.
As an independent member, allow me to say that the recent visit of our gracious Queen Elizabeth II and of her husband, Prince Philip, greatly warmed the hearts of Canadians, strengthened our convictions and

stimulated our efforts to safeguard the prerogatives and rights of each ethnical group in our beautiful country, in a spirit of frank co-operation and sincere understanding. (Text):
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister of Canada on his wonderful success in his victory of June 10. This victory was the result of tenacity and his hard-working spirit. I sincerely hope the whole of Canada will appreciate having him as their Prime Minister, and that his administration will contribute to a better Canada.
I should also like to congratulate the Prime Minister on his choice for the position of Speaker in this new parliament, as well as for his nomination of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) as Deputy Speaker. As we know, their duties are of great importance, but due to the fact that these hon. members are competent we are sure they will fulfil those important duties with great diligence, as their undeniably good record will reveal.
As an independent member of the house, I assure the Prime Minister that it will be a pleasure as well as a duty for me to support his government as much as possible and as long as his government presents measures which will contribute to bring peace and happiness in the homes of the Canadian people, and as long as they do not come into conflict with the sacred rights of my province and with the interests of my constituents.
(Translation) :
Mr. Speaker, it is with pride and pleasure that I say to this house that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) will go down in history as one of the greatest figures of any country. In my estimation, he is the very personification of frankness and sincerity. Everything about him bespeaks dignity. Through the prestige of his personality, no one will have contributed more to the great cause of national unity. On behalf of my electors, I congratulate him and I thank him.
May I, Mr. Speaker, commend the member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) who has so eloquently moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He shows promise of becoming one of the best speakers in the house. I also congratulate the seconder of the address, my hon. friend from Bona-venture (Mr. Arsenault). His electors will be proud of him and will be glad to be so worthily represented.
Mr. Speaker, several of the bills mentioned in the speech from the throne are bound to improve the lot of many Canadians, and I am glad this is so. However, allow me to endorse the views expressed by my colleagues

who spoke before me about the unstable situation of our agriculture in general. I think the government should give very special consideration to this matter and especially to family farming. The recession of farming across the country in general, is even more deplorable in my constituency, the county of Kamouraska.
Being mostly agricultural, this area is even more threatened than elsewhere. First, in so far as climate is concerned, there are barely five months of summer, and because winter lasts seven months or more, there is a sharp increase in production costs.
The farmers in my constituency live far from the great markets, pay high prices for the transport of their products and cannot afford hired help. Even their sons have to take outside jobs to earn money to pay for clothes, amusements and, of course, education. A supreme effort is urgently needed on the part of the government to establish as soon as possible, on a logical and reasonable basis, a price support on potatoes, and to adjust prices of butter and hogs, to mention Quebec products only.
I hope therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Quebec and the lower St. Lawrence will fare better under the new Conservative government. This is what everyone everywhere, from coast to coast, has been hoping since June 10. While Canada is a rich country, in her soil and sub-soil, to the point of arousing the envy of foreign interests, while it is a country that is still young and in full development, I would ask every member in this house why 80 per cent of our Canadian families are unable to secure the goods needed in these times and to provide the necessary education for their many children without going into the red and endangering their economic and family security?
The house spends a goodly part of its time considering representations of all kinds, from every part of the country and from every class of citizens, while the whole world is extolling Canada's wealth. Is it not paradoxical, Mr. Speaker? Where does the trouble lie? Does anyone know? If so, is there any possibility of any real and sincere attempt to correct it?
Fifty years ago, there was a production problem, which was solved by technology and mechanization. Today, the problem is one of distribution and marketing of the goods produced. The new social measures enacted by the government will alleviate to some degree the serious consequences of
The Address-Mr. Chabot the present problem, but I am afraid that nothing is going to be done about its basic cause. Governments will increasingly have to face a people suffering from philosophical and spiritual depression as well as from mechanical and materialistic hysteria.
For those two reasons, people will not restrain their greed in the face of so many products of science and progress, which means that the task of our present and future leaders will be extremely difficult. Social security legislation will become more and more necessary to offset less and less adequate wages.
By the force of circumstance, governments are more and more pressed to resort to compensatory legislation, but, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am afraid of the effects of paternalistic government side by side with anonymous private enterprise whose ultimate aim is profit. Because technical progress is more rapid than philosophical and educational advance, it creates a dangerous chaotic state in which governments have to be extremely cautious.
The chaos created by an industry progressing at 100 miles an hour, beside an agriculture which is still going at a leisurely 20 miles, will force governments to legislate so as to balance this disproportion. I welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne of legislation tending to improve such conditions.
This gap is even more deplorable in the eastern part of Quebec, because families there mainly depend for their living on agriculture and the lumber industry. Seventy to seventy-five per cent of our young people are leaving the land to go to the city for lack of industrial jobs.
This exodus is a social evil which should be stopped at all costs by stimulating smaller industries and by promoting the development of untapped natural resources. For instance, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the government's attention to the airport now being built in my county, near Notre Dame du Portage. The hopes of the people and local chambers of commerce in the counties of Kamouraska and Temiscouata are centred on this airport. This landing field is being built with funds voted by the last government and I hope that the present government will pass further legislation to facilitate an early completion of this project. In order to prove its usefulness and significance, I shall quote the words spoken by the hon. Leader of the Opposition at a meeting in St. Pascal during the last election campaign.

The Address-Mr. Chahot
I quote:
Stating he was very optimistic about the outcome of the current campaign, Mr. St. Laurent then referred to the construction work which is about to start on the future municipal airport. After describing this project as a substantial and justified improvement for Riviere du Loup, in the field of communications, the prime minister suggested that the Trans-Canada Airlines might include Riviere du Loup as a stopping point of one of its domestic air routes. Adding that our local airport might eventually be used by chartered aircraft, Mr. St. Laurent also revealed the existence of a project to operate a helicopter service between Riviere du Loup and Manoir Richelieu for the speedy transport of travellers and tourists.
The use of this airport would greatly help the economic development of our district, as stated by the former Prime Minister himself.
There has been for some time a great deal of talk about winter shipping on the St. Lawrence, from the gulf to Quebec. This project would help relieve winter unemployment and promote the completion of a dyke in deep water in the county of my hon. friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. J. P. St. Laurent), at Cacouna. Soundings with regard to this project have been undertaken by experts and it has been found that, because of the action of certain sea currents, the river at this point is, from natural causes, almost always free from ice. The building of the Notre Dame du Portage airfield and of this dyke in deep waters with the help of the government would be beneficial to the economy and industry of our district which is now suffering from an alarming depression.
If completed in the near future, these two projects would help us take advantage of the magnificent development on the north shore, just across the river. Our farmers would be able to dispose of their produce in a natural way, and our workers could travel more easily. Mr. Speaker, that part of Quebec which I represent in this house deserves special consideration from the present government, for this is the first time since confederation, that the constituency of Kam-ouraska has not been represented by a Liberal member. Having been a Liberal constituency for 90 years, the constituency of Kamouraska has now sent a new face to Ottawa. My constituents have the greatest confidence in their new member. And for that reason I would like to make out a strong case in this house for the need of generous government action with regard to those problems peculiar to my constituency and to my province.
Increased benefits have just been voted to our older citizens, to the blind, the disabled, and the veterans. Moreover, the western farmer will henceforth receive cash advances

for his grain. That is all well and good and I congratulate the government, even though the balancing of the budget may suffer thereby. The speech from the throne has forecast substantial increases to the benefit of agriculture in general. The farming population of this country is looking to Ottawa and expecting with greatest confidence the implementation of support prices calculated to increase their security.
I would ask the government not to forget the farmers who produce pulpwood. There are many of them in my constituency. From one year to the next they have no idea what price they will get for their wood. Those producers must be protected by an adequate support price so that they will not remain at the mercy of powerful large companies.
Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of speculation on the reasons for the great change brought about on June 10, 1957. In my humble opinion, if the present government is a Conservative one, it is because the people have understood that it would be more liberal in its social legislation. On the other hand, if the opposition is now made up of Liberals, it is because it was felt that the Liberals were or wished to be more conservative in intent and in action.
The recent increases voted for the benefit of our older citizens, our blind people, our disabled citizens and our veterans will be such as to bring comfort to thousands of Canadian homes. Should the government do nothing else, it would have proved its usefulness to the country.
We hear much talk in this house about Canadian unity. Unfortunately national unity is often seriously grieved in its heart and soul!
If the very few trouble-makers within both our great races in this country kept silent instead of taking advantage, for political and personal purposes, of certain prejudices as old as our country itself, national unity would fare better and there would be greater understanding between the majority of the citizens of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, one of the greatest dangers which threaten our modern civilization, possibly more than any nuclear weapon, is the licentious use being made of the great propaganda media, namely television, radio and the press, in the name of art, freedom of speech and of the press.
More and more, and for the sake of so-called freedom, the hearts and minds of our young people and even adults are being poisoned by the most disgusting publicity

given to crime, and by the stirring of the basest instincts of human nature through obscene and salacious stories.
It is the duty of the government to keep watch on those propaganda media so that they will not be used for the degradation of our society. Hon. members of this house should adopt the interpretation of the supreme court of the United States as to the precise meaning of the word "obscene", so that our judges may know what to think on this point. If in the name of art and freedom we allow our growing generation to degrade itself, we are aiding and abetting the disorders that will follow as a result of the imbalance of minds and of real values caused by a propaganda which knows no restriction in the detailed exposition of crime and lust.
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the increase of family allowances does not appear in the program for this session. My constituency is part of a section of this country where, according to a recent survey, the ratio of children below fifteen to the number of families is the highest of all Canada.
If family allowances were substantially increased, especially for children of twelve to eighteen years of age, I think it would be a good way to help universities and educational institutions, without encroaching upon constitutional rights. If an allowance of $12 to $15 a month was granted to any school child up to the age of 18, what a fine subsidy to education that would be without encroaching too much upon constitutional rights, especially when we know that education is an essential condition of our economic future. I hope the government intends to increase the family allowances soon.
I urge the government to make our unemployment insurance legislation more flexible so that it may be easier for bush workers to receive unemployment benefits. The government should also revise eligibility requirements for such benefits so that our bush workers will not be forced to accept inconsistent and inhuman working conditions as happens so often.
I would feel remiss in my duty if I concluded those few remarks without supporting my hon. friends who urged the government to equip this house with a system of simultaneous translation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, with the co-operation of all parties in this house, let us get together to give our country a distinctive Canadian flag, red and white, sealed with a maple leaf, so that every Canadian may salute that flag while singing, each in his own language, the joy, the glory and the expectations of Canada.
The Address-Mr. McLeod
When all Canadians are united around the same flag the different elements which make up our beautiful and great country will love and understand one another better and join in the fulfilment of the great destinies which Providence has assigned to them.

Mr. Speaker, like other members of this house I listened with a great deal of pleasure to the speeches made by the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the motion to adopt an address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do believe that the history-making event when that speech was delivered in person by our gracious Queen imbued hon. members and the mover and the seconder with a greater sense of responsibility.
I would go further and say that every member in this house seems to be showing a greater interest in the proceedings, due possibly to the fact that the responsibility for carrying out the program in this house has been placed on his or her shoulders by Her Gracious Majesty. Then again I am satisfied that a very wise choice has been made in the selection of our Speaker and his deputy, and that instead of congratulating those two hon. members I should congratulate this house on having such personable gentlemen in control of its proceedings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was dealing with certain statements which had been made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) in my riding. During the course of these remarks I drew attention to his statement relative to my neighbour to the south, Mr. Owen L. Jones, the former member for Okanagan Boundary, and I paid a personal tribute to that gentleman. I hope my hon. friends in the C.C.F. ranks across the way did not misunderstand me and attribute those words to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano because that hon. member in speaking of Mr. Jones described him as the man "to the south who babbled socialism."
I wish now to outline some of the problems with which our part of British Columbia is confronted and I am satisfied they are of such broad proportions that they affect the whole economy of Canada in many of its phases. In the first place I would point out that one problem which is developing and causing great concern to the various municipalities in the northern part of the interior is that with respect to future water supplies. It is perhaps rather peculiar to think and talk about a shortage of water in an area where we have such an abundance of lakes and rivers; however, it is not always so easy to bring that water to those points where it will do the most good. For this reason we now have an organization looking to the future when we anticipate a much larger concentration of population at which time additional supplies of water will be required not only for domestic purposes but also for irrigation. I refer to the organization known as the North Okanagan metropolitan

water board. This board is considering the whole problem of finding a suitable supply of water that can be provided to the various municipalities and will give them ample supplies on a gravity basis. Such a source is available. It is going to take a considerable amount of money to complete the exploratory engineering. I understand it will cost a minimum of $80,000.
In thinking of this project I cannot help but recall similar things that have been planned and then brought to completion under the P.F.R.A. regulations in parts of the prairie provinces. For this reason I make the plea, as I have made it yearly and perhaps more often since coming to this house, that we have some such plan of water distribution made available to the people of British Columbia. I would recommend as I have in the past that the word "prairie" be eliminated and that the name of this act with all its benefits-and I maintain that it has many benefits that can be applied to all parts of Canada-be changed to read, "National Farm Rehabilitation Act".
In our part of the interior of British Columbia we require extensions of experimental farm services. I am glad to say that during the past summer there has been some improvement. There has been some worth while extension of the services we have received and I will only continue my plea that this present government look into the program and accelerate the improvements that are being made thereunder.
Another thing about which we have heard a great deal and which has captured the imagination not only of the people of B.C. but of the whole of Canada is the development of power on the Columbia river. No part of British Columbia will benefit more directly from the development of power from that source than will my part of British Columbia and we are directly thinking, of course, of the Mica creek dam. During the past three or four years we have heard much about the problem of downstream benefits.
We had been given to understand that it was a matter of first importance to the late government and that swift action was being taken to secure a speedy settlement of the whole problem of downstream benefits on international rivers. We have not heard anything about any such action recently. In fact, questions put forward to elicit information in this respect have been casually brushed off by the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) with the evasive statement that there is nothing to report. We believe this is a matter of urgency and that the economy of the interior of British Columbia and the projected advance in that economy which we are sure could be 96698-761
The Address-Mr. McLeod forthcoming are entirely dependent on the development of power on the Columbia river. We have looked forward with great anticipation to prompt action by the government in solving the problem of downstream benefits. In the past this was given prior consideration but now we are told that before anything can be done we must have the report of the Borden commission.
I would point out that we do not require a Borden commission to convince us of the great benefits that would accrue from the development of this project nor do we require that commission to persuade us of the need of developing it at an early date. Any delay in bringing this matter to the state where work can be proceeded with is nothing less than a blanket, and a wet blanket at that, withholding development of the whole interior of British Columbia.
As was mentioned by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) the other day, we too have an airfield problem in practically every town in the interior, but there is a slightly different point of view from which we may look upon the development of airfields in our area. At the present time the civil defence authorities have designated the interior as a receiving centre in case of trouble or attack on the densely populated coastal areas. If these events should occur and if it becomes necessary to move the hundreds of thousands of people from the coastal areas to the interior, how is it going to be done? We do not have roadways and we receive no assistance from the federal government to provide them. In any case the coming method of quick evacuation and speedy travel is by air making better facilities imperative.
Therefore, I would suggest that this government take a new look at the matter of airfield development. Look at the future prospects of such progress, such development and travel and give the three important areas in my community every consideration. I am referring to the airfield at Ellison which, though in my riding, is maintained and kept up by the city of Kelowna. Nevertheless, this is becoming a great centre, and we hope it will be a great centre in coast-to-coast transportation if and when the Canadian Pacific Air Lines gets a charter to fly to Montreal. At the present time it is planned to make the Ellison field an important stop in the air transportation service between Vancouver and Edmonton.
The city of Vernon has a small field, but a splendid area is available to the north which has been inspected by officials of the Department of Transport and which has been pronounced to be one of the best in the interior of British Columbia. In order for the city to get appropriate rights to the land so that it can be held in reserve for

The Address-Mr. McLeod airport services it is necessary that they should know the over-all national program of this government in regard to the development of civil flying in this part of the country.
We have a field in Revelstoke on which thousands of dollars have been spent locally together with grants from the federal department. In the past couple of years promises have been given that a further $10,000 or $12,000 would be granted in order to complete the runway but, for some reason or other, the powers that be have seen fit to cancel those appropriations just when it seemed we were on the threshold of receiving them.
I cannot let this opportunity pass without referring to unemployment. Here, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I stand 100 per cent behind the remarks made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) in the house the other day. We are not talking blue ruin; we have no fear complex because we know that with proper government policies, financial and fiscal, the problems that are facing the country at the present time can be solved. All that we are asking is that the government give serious consideration to those problems as they arise. I do believe that the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is doing the best within his power but I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that he is not the one who is responsible for unemployment. He is the minister who, under the unemployment insurance service and under the employment service, provides perhaps some measure of alleviation but he has nothing whatever to do with unemployment. The department of government that has more to do with unemployment is the Department of Public Works, which announces that public spending is being cut; that public buildings are being shelved in general. I maintain that in a time like this when we have unemployment the government, instead of talking retrenchment, instead of talking economy, instead of holding up the public works program, should be accelerating them and should be spending more money into circulation.
I hold in my hand the October 28 issue of the Vernon News, which contains this headline:
Unemployment Up In City
Doubles Over 1956
Official figures from the national employment service indicate that unemployment has more than doubled. The article goes on to say:
Number of unemployed persons registered at the national employment service is 2.6 times higher in October this year than over the same month in 1956.
I am not quoting these figures because I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, or because I want to

create a feeling of fear and pessimism, since I have every confidence in the future of British Columbia and in the economy of British Columbia, provided that the present government will take the proper steps to give it a chance to progress and to develop.
The other day we had a very clear analysis of another problem that is developing in the province of British Columbia and which will contribute to the unemployment situation. That analysis was made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and I should like to congratulate him on the clear and forthright manner in which the problem was presented to the house. I am going to back him up, Mr. Speaker, and ask this government, in the face of this serious threat of 800 more people being added to the rolls of the unemployed, a problem which is becoming increasingly greater across Canada, what they intend to do about it? Do they intend to sit idly by and say, we are doing everything possible? I am going to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this is one thing that requires and demands the attention of the government before the whole unemployment problem in British Columbia is aggravated by an additional 800 men. In this respect we were shown how it would actually save this government money by subsidizing or paying the necessary amount of money to keep the mine in operation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take you back for a few moments to the campaign which preceded the election of June 10. At that time most Canadians were beginning to feel the pinch and the effects of the tight money policy. This tight money policy, as was said in the house the other day, was hitting them where it hurt. Rightly or wrongly the people of Canada believed that the tight money policy was responsible in large measure for the increase in the cost of living. They believe it is responsible for the slow-down in municipal projects; it is responsible for higher taxes in municipal and school districts, owing to the high cost of borrowing and the high interest rates on money which they require to borrow. It is responsible for the slow-down in basic industries, especially the lumber industry in British Columbia, which has shrunk by more than 30 per cent in gross income during the past year. It has brought about difficult employment conditions and a tightening of credit that has made it impossible for the small businessman and the small farmer to secure the necessary funds to carry on.
All opposition parties, including the great Conservative party, played this up during the last campaign but none of us gave it more attention than did the Conservatives. I am going to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that

the Conservatives made pledges which will never be forgotten. They said that if they were returned and placed in office they would take immediate steps to alleviate the tight money situation. The people of Canada have not forgotten that pledge.
I would like to ask you, Mr. Speaker, what has this government actually done? Minister after minister has risen in his place and said that the government has taken all necessary steps but I should like them to name one thing that this government has done as a government. It is true that there has been a lowering of the interest rate, but was that the result of government action? Or was it the natural action of the Bank of Canada? This is something I should like to hear explained. The Conservative party now in power condemned the Bank of Canada just as loudly as the rest of us and also condemned the previous government for allowing themselves to be placed in a position where they were dominated by the Bank of Canada.
But again I ask, what is the change? I should like to have seen, and I think the people of Canada would like to have seen, some action by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the government whereby they would stand up to the Bank of Canada and say: Here is government policy, and this is what we want to see made effective in Canada. Instead, what do we learn? We learn that there is no difference of opinion between the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Another trump card of the Conservative party during the campaign was the question of the supremacy of parliament. Far too many promises were made, promises which the government is finding it quite hard to live up to. They promised that the tight money policy would be alleviated at once. They promised that the supremacy of parliament would be restored and that the rights of members would be protected. I am just going to refer briefly to what I think about the whole question of the supremacy of parliament. I make the broad statement that never in my experience has there been so much flouting of the rights of private members as there has been during the past month. I have never seen such evasion on the part of ministers and very seldom have I seen a prime minister go out and make speeches on policy and proposed policy of the government before presenting such policies to parliament, which should be first to learn of all matters of legislation.
I see that my time is growing short, Mr. Speaker. I should have liked to go considerably further in discussing the matter of parliamentary supremacy because I know
The Address-Mr. McLeod there is much that could be said. However, I shall analyse the situation a little further. What were the people looking for when they voted as they did on June 10? I maintain that the electors of Canada were looking for an alternative. What did they get? What alternative has the government offered in any policy they are considering at the present time? I simply ask that question, and I know that the people of Canada are asking that question, too.
In what way are the policies of the present government different from the policies of the government which the people of Canada rejected in the hope of finding an alternative? I could go on and elaborate but I will simply take a couple of items that are or have been on the order paper. I am very glad to see that there is a resolution extending assistance to the agriculturists of Canada. I think everyone knows that legislation in that respect is long overdue and is one of the most important things required in this country. But what about the price support program? In what way is it an alternative to the program which the Liberals have had for a good many years? The government says that it is going to be enlarged and broadened, but the same policies are going to be in effect. Is that an alternative? Is it anything different from what was offered before?
Reference can be made to the legislation passed by the house dealing with welfare. Is it an alternative? Is there any different approach? I say to hon. members that it is the same approach. We are not satisfied with the alternative for which the people of Canada voted and what they hoped to get last June 10. We also read about trade. I was greatly encouraged by statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that commonwealth and British trade were going to be increased. There was a lot of talk about it. I like many other Canadians looked hopefully to the government. What happened? The minute that Britain said to Canada, all right, Canada, if you want to trade with Britain we are prepared to go the whole way and give you every opportunity to trade with us. What happened? Immediately the government started back-pedalling. In effect they said to the people of Canada, and to England, we did not mean all this about trade with Britain; we were just talking so do not take it too seriously. That is the way that the people of Canada size up the situation.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that I have only one minute left. I have an announcement that I should like to make. Today we shall be taking the main vote on the motion before us and I should like to read to the house a statement endorsed by the Social Credit members.

The Address-Mr. Taylor
In regard to our stand on the main motion the leader of this group pointed out that in order to solve our economic problems it will be necessary to bring about certain reforms in the existing financial system. We moved an amendment to that effect which was defeated. We are still of the same opinion. However, we believe that the government should be given an opportunity to show what it can do in dealing with the problems of the nation as outlined in the speech from the throne. We will therefore, Mr. Speaker, support the main motion when the vote comes later today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with humility that I rise in my place for the first time in this distinguished house to continue the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. You will recall, sir, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) honoured a westerner to move the address in reply to the speech from the throne. He delivered a most fitting address and referred, as was natural, to his illustrious father who passed away some time ago. Later in the debate my colleague, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney), spoke about his father who likewise served so well in the house but who did not live to see his son honoured in this parliament.
Fortunately, my father is living and has been observing his son carry on his parliamentary duties. While in Ottawa dad was interviewed on television about his hockey career and I gave him moral support. Today he is in my rooting section and I feel he will get as great a thrill out of these proceedings as he ever got out of the alleged back-handed goal scored over 40 years ago in this very city.
There is another person whom I should like to see in the gallery of the house. I refer to the mother of the Prime Minister. It is my understanding, sir, that she is the only mother in Canadian history who ever saw her son become prime minister of this country. Perhaps in the near future she can be present to see her famous son lead the government.
I appreciate this honour and opportunity of speaking in this august chamber and the privilege of representing the constituency of Vancouver-Burrard. I think it is the usual custom to offer congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, upon your appointment to high office. I did not know until the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) pointed it out that you were born in Red Deer, Alberta. Long before I came to know the name of Roland Michener, I knew well Michener hill which is on the outskirts of Red Deer. The hill is as prominent to the citizens of Red Deer as Mr. Speaker will be to this house.

In congratulating you, sir, I should like to congratulate others. When I think of the physical disabilities of the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod and of how he has overcome them, which was obvious during the opening of parliament, I must say that he deserves special commendation.
I will never forget the opening of parliament in October, 1957 as the majesty of it all unfolded itself before our very eyes. I am sure that when I get back to Vancouver many of my constituents will want my personal observations on the activities in the house. My report, sir, will be in most glowing terms. I personally appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister took time to refer in such a fitting way to the late Dr. Blair who died a few days after the recent election. His remarks were followed by those of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) and in turn by those of other hon. members. This served notice upon the newcomers that if you serve well in this house, all will remember you in such a nice manner.
I was glad to see the Prime Minister pay personal tribute to another member, namely the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) upon his winning the Nobel peace prize. You will recall, sir, that the Prime Minister crossed the floor of the house, shook hands first with the Leader of the Opposition and then turned to his left and shook hands vigorously with the hon. member for Algoma East. That is what newcomers wanted to see, namely a great leader paying tribute in such a nice manner for work well done. Sometimes I think that the Prime Minister has a heart bigger than himself. Probably it is because of that that the nation decided to "follow John" in the last election.
I want to report to my constituents about the fitting and kind remarks made by my Prime Minister concerning the retirement as leader of the hon. member for Quebec East. My constituents have great respect for the Leader of the Opposition. I have always looked forward to hearing him speak. His decorum and deportment set a mark for us all to attain. We Canadians have been so fortunate in having leaders like the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. While I am not of the same political faith as the latter, I have always joined in the thunderous applause that attends his appearance at meetings of the Canadian Bar Association and other such meetings.
Before commenting on the speech from the throne, may I also refer to my predecessor, Dr. MacDougall, who represented my constituency of Vancouver-Burrard and who passed away in this house prior to the last election. I never knew him personally but everywhere

I go in this house people who knew him have a kind word for him. If I can be remembered as he was I shall feel that my service here in this house was not in vain.
Before the election I received from one of my constituents a poem which reads as follows:
To "follow John" I'm not content Until I find which way he went.
After the election there was a further poem:
Now having boldly followed John And made our wishes clear,
This is the thought we dwell upon-
Where do we go from here?
Upon reading the speech from the throne, the nation knows which way John went and which way he goes from here. Members of the opposition say that he has not kept faith with the electorate. I suggest, sir, that the Prime Minister has kept faith. Undoubtedly the opposition policy this session will be "irritation without challenge".
I should like to refer to an article written in the Vancouver Sun by Mr. Elmore Phil-pott, a Liberal, who in the last parliament sat but a few seats from mine. Mr. Philpott wrote:
The 1957 speech from the throne is an historic document for several reasons. But the one which means most to the people of Canada is that the Conservatives have spectacularly kept their main election promises.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has not only itemized the main points on which he was morally bound to take action at this session, but he also outlined intended action in several other matters which might well have been postponed for the future without giving justification for this cry of bad faith.
The whole country, regardless of party preference, should be delighted to see this proof that the old party of Sir John A. Macdonald has thus demonstrated that its official title of "Progressive" Conservatives has taken on new meaning for the whole Canadian nation.
Mr. Frank Bernard, a member of the Vancouver board of trade and, I suggest, a man who represents the feeling of most British Columbia businessmen, is delighted that the Prime Minister has seen fit to strike a royal commission to inquire into important industrial matters relating to power. The appointment of Mr. Leon Ladner of British Columbia, lawyer and industrialist, is most appropriate.
Senior citizens in my riding, like Mrs. Emilie Campbell, welcome the relief in higher old age pensions.
Citizens throughout my riding will be gratified that action is to be taken concerning power on the Columbia river.
The speech from the throne had hardly been concluded before the Prime Minister added two new planks to his sessional legislative program. One dealt with federal subsidies on shipments of maritime coal destined
The Address-Mr. Taylor for power generation on the east coast. The aim was cheaper power to attract industry to that area. The other was abolition of the debate-limiting Commons closure rule; and tomorrow the Prime Minister will add further planks to his program. As one rookie M. P. jokingly said to me: "Brother, watch John; you ain't seen nothin' yet!".
Many of the problems which exist in my constituency are common to all. Many of the hon. members who have spoken have made reference to them and I do not intend to repeat what they have said. However, I wish to add a comment about reforms in the immigration set-up. I feel that there is a need to review and amend the act, the regulations and the administration thereof. Time does not allow me to discuss all the suggestions I have in mind but may I suggest one. Immigration appeals should be heard by an immigration appeal board, and not by the minister. For a generation now persons having immigration problems have approached the immigration minister. Often these people are represented by members of this house, and far too often the cases in the past were disposed of after some informal and injudicious hearing, tinged often with partisan feelings.
If a proper administrative set-up is provided for the hearing of immigration cases, no member would again find himself importuned to interpose in administrative rulings. An applicant for admission should be able to test his admissibility under a proper administration set-up. If he does not qualify he is excluded; if he does qualify he is to be admitted. If then, there are persons who have been excluded but whose cases involve unusual and compelling circumstances a private bill should be applied for. In applying for a private bill all members of the house would know who was applying and what were the special circumstances. Open and fair hearings together with publication of immigration decisions would revolutionize the present set-up.
Before leaving this subject may I suggest that careful consideration be given to the many recommendations passed by the Canadian Bar Association dealing with immigration practices and procedures. Much praise is due to John McDonald, an Ottawa lawyer, who worked tirelessly to bring about these recommendations. He championed a cause which he conscientiously felt was right and it is to be hoped that it will not be long before the suggestions of his committee will be incorporated into the immigration laws of this country.

The Address-Mr. Taylor
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) is considering many problems relating to television. I feel that we have a unique situation in Vancouver; the government has granted one television outlet in this area of over one-half million people. If you do not want to watch this station, then the alternative stations are all United States stations. Within television range are five United States channels or stations which send out splendid programs to the large audience in my area. The learned Mr. Fowler felt that there was a danger of Canadians becoming engulfed by United States television. We in Vancouver were engulfed long ago and the situation at this time, I suggest, could hardly be worse. To partially correct the situation in my area I would suggest that additional Canadian private stations be permitted to operate at the earliest possible date.
The financial statement of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the year ending March 1957 is a story of deficit and debt. The fact that a government agency fails to show a profit should not evoke surprise; other government departments and agencies cost the public large sums of money. It costs money to run the armed forces, the police force, the customs and postal departments; the only difference is that these undertakings come under the heading of public utilities whereas broadcasting, like newspaper publishing, is quite able to subsist, and subsist usefully, under a system of private enterprise with no drain on the public treasury.
I suggest that wherever private enterprise can do the job and do it well the government should not be in that field. I personally like the C.B.C. station in Vancouver; there is much to commend it, but when I realize that under private enterprise I would get pretty well the same, if not better programs at no expense whatsoever, to me, then I have serious misgivings about the continuing interference of the government in this field.
I believe there is a useful function to be performed by a publicly-owned broadcasting system in assisting such things as educational programs. The government can also assist with respect to the broadcasting of serious music and the drama which has an appeal, admittedly, too limited to justify broadcasting commercially. However, none of these functions require the operation of a broadcasting machine running several radio and television networks, with 30 of its own stations, and employing 6,000 people at a cost to the country of nearly $40 million per year.
Then there is another matter which I would like to mention. The last links in the trans-Canada highway between Golden, British


Columbia and Banff are being built and the highway through the mountainous territory is expected to be completed next fall. I suggest that real assistance be given to the provinces in the establishment of all kinds of tourist facilities including outdoor camping grounds, certainly in this area, and probably coast to coast on the trans-Canada highway.
Investment by the senior government in this field is investment in something which is definitely Canadian. There is no danger of engulfment here as there is in television; there is no danger of competition. Investment here will, I suggest, bring far greater rewards than in the field of television. Investment in our parks, the finest in the world, will bring about lasting rewards. Public investment in television will, in my opinion, not attain that end.
Having referred to the national highways and to the question of tourists, may I suggest that the federal government give consideration to classifying the tourist trade as an industry so that operators may borrow from the industrial development bank. On the one hand the tourist trade is acknowledged as the third largest industry in Canada but, on the other hand, no adequate recognition is given so that resort operators can borrow from approved sources. Because the tourist dollar is so important to Canada all possible assistance should be given to the resort and hotel operators.
Now may I refer to one thing which has upset the friendliness and amiability of the house. I refer to the bitter address of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I was sorry to hear his speech about alleged racial and religious differences. He accused the party of Sir John A. Macdonald of all sorts of things. To a westerner this is upsetting and I feel that I can speak for all newcomers in the house in hoping that such bitterness will not be continued.
If I was disheartened by what the hon. member for Laurier said I was delighted by the activity of another French Canadian. A few Saturdays ago my wife and I went to Montreal where we saw the hockey game between Chicago and Montreal. We saw Maurice "the Rocket" Richard, score his 500th goal in a blaze of glory.

speechtext: You were lucky.
