speechtext:
We rose with the 15,000 people, French and English Canadians, to cheer the wonderful Rocket. There was no disunity there. Nor was there throughout the sporting fraternity of the nation on that night.
Everyone loves to visit the grand province of Quebec; it has a charm all its own and the friendliness of its people adds a cubit to

Canada's stature. What French and English have in common as Canadians is far more than the differences which divide them. With so much to be done, let us get on with the job and forget our minor differences.
In conclusion I would like to remind hon. members that engraved in stone over the main door of this building are the words:
The wholesome sea is at her gates;
Her gates both east and west.
Keep your eyes, Mr. Speaker, on the western gates. There is in that area the fastest industrial growth in all Canada. In the past 15 years the population of British Columbia has grown 71 per cent, compared with a national average of 35 per cent and business has been keeping pace with that expansion.
Mr. Speaker, October and November of 1957 have been thrilling months for me. I saw Her Majesty open Canada's parliament for the first time; I made my first appearance in the Supreme Court of Canada, and I have made my first speech in the house. I will always be grateful to the people of Vancouver-Burrard for making all this possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are all very grateful to Her Majesty the Queen for having come to Canada to take part in the opening proceedings of this session of parliament by reading in person the address which is now under debate.
I should like, in accordance with custom and because of my long relationship with him, to extend to Mr. Speaker, as other hon. members have done, my sincere congratulations upon his having been selected by all hon. members of this house to act as their Speaker. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) proposed Mr. Speaker's name to hon. members he referred to the reply which the Times newspaper made to Lord Palmerston who had inquired what were the necessary qualities of a person who was to occupy the chair as Speaker at Westminster. The Times replied: "Imperturbability, good temper, tact, urbanity, and, if possible, a training in the law." I think we have all recognized after four weeks that the Speaker has other qualities, too, and that pre-eminent among these is the quality of fairness and impartiality.
I should like to offer my congratulations also to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) for his excellent maiden speech when he proposed the motion that is before us. Those of us who were members here at the same time as his father could not help but feel that he not only did honour to himself but to his father's name.
The Address-Hon. Paul Martin It must have been a matter of deep satisfaction to his mother who sat in the gallery that day to realize that her son had begun his public life, in this house, under such happy and successful circumstances.
(Translation):
To the hon. member for Bonaventure I also offer my sincere congratulations, not for what he said but rather for the ease with which he said it.
(Text):
Today I propose to deal with certain observations made last night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I will not attempt to cover all he said, because he did traverse quite a wide field. I want to deal mainly with that portion of his speech which took up least time to say but which, I should have thought, would have comprised the major portion of his contribution to our deliberations. I refer to the proposals made by the Prime Minister and those of Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom in the matter of trading relations between these two nations. But the hon. gentleman in that careful, moderate manner of his, began by saying that the problems of the government were considerable, largely because of the inheritance from the administration directed by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the opposition. And he listed these inheritances in detail.
I will simply say by way of reply that no government, certainly in this day of complex arrangements, can hope to be free of important problems of a domestic and international character covering all aspects of the life of the nation or of the world. No manipulation of words by the Minister of Finance can alter the fact that when the present government took office late in June it did so as the government of a country whose prosperity was never higher, whose prospects were never brighter, whose prestige was never so great among the nations of the world. And so, if in the meantime, certain economic disquietudes have arisen, no one with a sense of fairness will argue that this administration, in office for five months, is responsible for this particular uneasiness in its entirety. But I think we have the right, and indeed, the duty, just as did the Prime Minister when he sat on this side of the house, to charge the government in relation to the disturbing situation now confronting us. No amount of palliation will or can overlook the fact that at the present time whatever may be the cause there are disturbing economic factors-how fundamental I do not know-which affect the material well-being of many hundreds of thousands of people in our country.

The Address-Hon. Paul Martin
In agriculture, low prices; in our industrial life, much unemployment; these are factors which not only the government but all of us have to consider, and it is therefore of the greatest importance that we should give serious consideration to an analysis of the policies of the government in respect of a matter which fundamentally, has occasioned much uncertainty and which in the course of the next few months could have a definite bearing on the economic progress of Canada and a great effect on the level of employment in our country. So many people in their economic lives are affected by the policies of any government in the matter of its trading relations with other countries.
This government has made much of its trading policies. Indeed, during the course of the election and long before in this house the Minister of Finance in particular spoke of the desirability of promoting a greater measure of commonwealth trade as a means of stimulating the lifeblood of our economy. Last night, looking toward those of us who sit on your left, Mr. Speaker, he said: "The fact is that hon. gentlemen opposite do not like the commonwealth." I venture to suggest to my hon. friend, my classmate whom I have known longer perhaps than anyone in this house that a common appreciation of the great purposes of the commonwealth of nations is not promoted in this country by alternately blowing hot and cold in the matter of closer relations between this country and the commonwealth in the economic or other spheres. By its brusque and belittling reaction to a serious proposal put forward by the United Kingdom, this government I submit with respect, has done a grave injury to the commonwealth.
It has shown it is willing to exploit the kindly sentiments most Canadians feel for the United Kingdom and for other commonwealth countries like Ceylon, India and Pakistan, let alone the countries of Australasia but unwilling nevertheless to take the most elementary steps towards giving practical expression to those sentiments when an element of political risk to itself or financial injury to some of its supporters appears.
Now, the Prime Minister said during the recent election that one of his aims would be the holding of a commonwealth economic and trade conference. And because of arrangements made by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) the present Prime Minister shortly after the election with the good will of all Canadians went to Great Britain for the purpose of participating at his first conference of prime ministers of the commonwealth.
If we can gather an accurate impression from the press both in the United Kingdom


and Canada his presence and vigourous approach in this particular matter seems to have captivated public attention in the United Kingdom, but one of the most amazing things it seems to me is that a careful perusal of the communique issued after the prime ministers conference makes no reference whatsoever to a proposal by the Prime Minister of Canada for an economic and trade conference with the commonwealth countries. Could it be that the prime minister of Australia, the prime minister of Great Britain, the prime ministers of Ceylon and of Pakistan and India wanted to make sure what kind of conference it was going to be? Perhaps they bore in mind the words of Sir Robert Borden that there is nothing wrong with a conference except that conferences seldom produce good results unless the parties conferring each know what they want to achieve and there is some measure of agreement in advance on the objective. I think that is a very important consideration particularly for Canada at the present time.
What is the position of other countries visa-vis Canada? We were reminded the other day by Mr. Macmillan in the statement he made at the Guild Hall that what Britain wanted was capital assistance. Likewise those of us who have had any experience in government know-as I am sure is the case with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and the Minister without Portfolio from Newfoundland (Mr. Browne) who has just returned from Asia- that the great need of the Asian members of the commonwealth is for capital assistance, capital aid in carrying out their projects. Are we going to be able to meet that objective when this conference takes place? Are we going to be able to offer to these countries the kind of assistance which in so far as they are concerned is the motive, the reason, the raison d'etre, for an economic trade conference with commonwealth countries?
We all remember there was another conference held in this very chamber in 1932, the imperial economic conference convened at the suggestion of the then prime minister of Canada, the late Lord Bennett. With regard to that particular conference it is debatable even now whether it contributed much to the unity of the commonwealth itself and there is little doubt as to whether it did not contribute to a deterioration in the relations between many nations of the world. But it can be said for the late Lord Bennett that when he invited other governments to a conference he had something for them to confer about.

It would be extremely interesting to know whether or not before he went to the prime ministers conference the Prime Minister of Canada had forewarned the commonwealth countries in the usual and customary diplomatic way of the kind of proposal which he intended to put forward at that conference. There could be no objection, indeed there is everything to be gained by commonwealth statesmen meeting from time to time to discuss common problems, political, economic and international, but a conference called for a special purpose, particularly an economic purpose, presupposes care in preparation and a serious amount of consideration as to the likely outcome unless danger and damage are to be caused instead of resulting in some constructive situation.
It is a simple fact that in our free economic system there are only a few things that governments can do to change the normal course of trade. One is to put up barriers against imports whether by means of tariffs or otherwise. Another is to take down such barriers as already exist. Mr. Bennett in 1932 had a definite plan and part of that plan was to put up barriers against imports from non-empire sources. That was a definite objective; but what is the objective of the present government in this particular?
The Prime Minister of Canada returned to this country after the prime ministers conference and the first thing he did was to go and meet the journalists and newspapermen who are in this building, serving this nation with distinction. During the course of his conference with them he said that he was prepared to make a proposal which would have a great bearing on our economic relationships both with the United States and with Great Britain. He would shift 15 per cent of Canadian purchases in the United States to the United Kingdom. We have since estimated, of course, that the total of this shift would come to at least $625 million but this was not indicated by the Prime Minister at that time. However, what I think is most amazing is that the proposal should have been made, not in the United Kingdom, not at the prime ministers conference where as far as our Prime Minister was concerned the dominant theme was commonwealth trade but outside of that conference in Canada immediately after his return from the United Kingdom.
That raises, I think, legitimate doubt as to the circumstances of the birth of that particular idea. Was it the result of careful planning and consideration? Was it the result of preparatory work that had been done by the Prime Minister's economic and trade advisors? Or was it just an idea that sud-96698-77J
The Address-Hon. Paul Martin denly came to him, one that had the quality of the spectacular, one that would fit in with his enthusiasm, understandable as it was, at the moment? Was it, as has been suggested, a reckless idea; or was it one that had been carefully considered?
One has reason to doubt whether the suggestion really deserves the designation of "proposal" for not once during the course of the present session of parliament has any hon. member sitting on the treasury benches made any reference to this proposal except that made last night by the Minister of Finance who simply said, ''Give us time".
He did not say how long. "Give us time and we will provide for a shift in Canadian purchases from the United States to Great Britain".
That was the only mention of this proposal made by any member of the treasury since this session began. We believe from the communique that flowed from the conference in Washington, when Canadian and United States ministers conferred, that the proposal, or the idea of a shift in Canadian purchases, was really something not to be taken too seriously; it was something in the very long term, in any event. Because of this assurance, apparently, United States cabinet ministers were able to say with satisfaction, understandable satisfaction, "Well, if this shift is not really going to take place for a long time we have no hesitation in giving you assurances on some points of concern to Canada".
But long before the Washington conference what had happened? Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom had taken this matter seriously. They knew that a proposal such as that which the Prime Minister had in mind was one that could not be implemented under the terms of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. And so the British government came forward with a formal proposal in Ottawa, through the chancellor of the exchequer, after the conference at Mont Tremblant.
We have the assurance of the Minister of Finance in that very exhaustive report he gave us two or three weeks ago about these various conferences, when he said that the first formal presentation of the British free trade proposal was given some time during the visit of the chancellor of the exchequer to Ottawa after the conference at Mont Tremblant; but he did not deny that on September 10 the minister of agriculture, Mr. Amory, had discussed the British proposal with him. We do know that Sir David Eccles, the president of the board of trade, was in Washington and had discussions with officials of the government of Canada about this very matter.

The Prime Minister has denied that when the president of the hoard of trade was at the United Nations, on the occasion of the Prime Minister's visit, there was any discussion between them with regard to Britain's free trade proposal. Well, Mr. Speaker, one must accept and one readily accepts the word of the Prime Minister; but nevertheless no mem: ber of the government can seriously take the position that the first real intimation of this very important proposal, perhaps the most important proposal ever made by one commonwealth government to another in the matter of trade, had not been brought to the attention of this administration long before that eventful evening within the luxurious surroundings of Mont Tremblant.
Then we are told by the Minister of Finance in a speech he made in New York that the assurances which he had been given by his counterparts in the government of the United States were not fully satisfactory and so we have this change of position. At one moment they are satisfied with their talks at Washington and a few weeks later the expression in New York, with these ministers absent, by the Minister of Finance is that after all the assurances were not as satisfactory as he would have liked. Apparently our ministers were treated in Washington by the Americans seemingly just as my hon. friend had treated the British at Mont Tremblant, because, if this proposal had been brought to the attention of the administration on September 10, as he admits it was, it deserved serious study and consideration.
How was it treated? Well, we really do not know because the Minister of Finance is reported as merely having said that it was laden with difficulties; there was no sympathetic consideration even offered or suggested. We do not know yet, therefore, what this British proposal was in detail; but obviously the Minister of Finance himself does know because he spoke of it at least at Mont Tremblant. We do know what it was in broad outline. It was a proposal to lower the barriers of trade and, as 1 have said, there are only two ways in free countries to influence the course of trade. One is to lower barriers and the other is to raise them. As parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade both the British and ourselves are pretty well stopped from raising new barriers against non-commonwealth countries.
Now, surely, it was open to, and it was the duty of a government that speaks so feverishly of its love for the commonwealth to the point of trying to create division to see that that proposal, having in mind all of its implications, would receive friendly attention and not downright dismissal. It is certainly a

proposal that would have been accepted by Sir John A. Macdonald. It is a proposal that would give free entry to the British market of all products in Canada, including automobiles. It would have meant free entry on a preferred basis because British restrictions against the United States, our principal competitors, would remain unchanged. In the trading situation which is now developing it would have meant more; for Britain is about to obtain free entry to all the markets of western Europe, France, Germany, Italy, the low countries, Scandinavia. Our metals and forest products, our wheat, which is now going to Britain in substantial quantities, would be sold in larger quantities to their flour mills and their factories to increase their production in order to sell more of their products on the European market. It would mean that Canada would get entry into the European free-trade area. In any event, it is a proposal put forward by a friendly government, and it should have received the kind of treatment which it deserved, particularly having in mind the provocation for that proposal, namely the suggestion made by the Prime Minister of Canada in the press gallery to Canadian newspapermen after the prime ministers' conference.
I would like to make this observation in passing, Mr. Speaker. We asked the Minister of Finance to give us some details of the proposal of the Canadian Prime Minister with regard to this shifting of purchases from one friendly country to another. I asked him to table the proposal of Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and his reply was that no one should know better than the interrogator, myself, how improper it would be for a minister of the crown to table such a document. That recalls the words of the Minister of Finance when he sat on this side of the house. He criticized my leader, then the prime minister, about the kind of position we were going to take at a prime ministers' conference in London several years ago. Here is what the Minister of Finance said:
If parliamentary Institutions enjoyed here in Ottawa the health that they ought to enjoy, no Canadian prime minister would go to an important commonwealth conference without having first invited a discussion in parliament on the position that he was going to take on behalf of his country in the deliberations of that conference.
This is what he said on the eve of the Mont Tremblant conference:
For a number of reasons the arguments to be advanced by the Canadian government in favour of a commonwealth trade and economic conference were on the secret list and would remain so.
If my hon. friend's words had validity when he was in opposition, Mr. Speaker, surely those words afford justification for my asking him to give us more precise information about the proposal of his own

The Address-Hon. Paul Martin
Prime Minister as well as the proposal made by Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
But what about this proposal of the Prime Minister? Is it a practical thing? Is it desirable? Is it not something that should be debated in the house? The Prime Minister is the author of it. He spoke early in this debate. He made no reference whatsoever to his proposal or, for that matter, to any aspect of our trading relations with any friendly or other country.
Let us examine this proposal to shift purchases from the United States to another friendly country, in this case the United Kingdom. We all respect the judgment of a former distinguished public servant of Canada, the former assistant deputy minister of finance, now head of the department of economics at the University of British Columbia. Here is what Professor John Deutsch had to say about this idea of shifting from one traditional or well-established trading channel to another:
We want prosperity but we fear the American trade on which it's based. We can't have it both ways. We can either develop our country ourselves and accept a lower rate of growth and prosperity or else we must do business with the United States.
This proposal for a shift means taking business away from our best customer. We do not want to take business away from our best customer. We want to increase trade with Great Britain. There is no one in the house or in the country who does not want to do that. Our objective should be to sell as much as we can to the United States in return for which there must be purchases and at the same time to build up our total volume of trade with all commonwealth and other countries.
But we talk about unemployment. I live in a city where there are now over 14,000 men out of work. English automobiles can come into Canada free of duty. Canadian automobiles cannot now enter Great Britain free of duty. I do not say that this is a fully acceptable proposal but I say it is one which on its very face deserves careful examination. I do not believe that we are contributing to the economic strength of this nation by disturbing, on the basis of ill-considered consideration, important trading relations that amount to almost $4 billion in their totality.
I do not believe that we should overlook the statement of the president of the board of trade made the other day in the United Kingdom that he had grave doubts that it would be possible in the foreseeable future for Great Britain, in the face of great demands made on her by European countries, to sell goods to Canada in the amount suggested by this 15 per cent shift. But let us look at
the future. We hope to build in this country a growing nation giving added economic strength and well-being to our people, and one of the ways by which we are going to do that is not only to improve the domestic but also to improve the external market. And the United States is a very important market, no matter what anyone, for sentimental or other reasons, may think, as was stated the other day by the chancellor of the exchequer himself.
In 1956 our exports of goods and services to the United States amounted to nearly two-thirds of our total exports. While there will be fluctuations from time to time, it seems probable that over the long pull the United States will continue to require increasing quantities of our principal exports to that country-newsprint, lumber, nickel, copper, lead, zinc, aluminum, iron ore, asbestos, gypsum and in the future we hope large quantities of oil and gas. These are the materials in which the United States sooner or later will be deficient and which we will have in abundance.
It seems likely, therefore, that not only will our exports to the United States increase considerably in absolute terms but that such exports may account for as much as 70 per cent or three-quarters of the total exports of this country in the years to come. The probability that our exports to the United States will increase is one of the important reasons why we can be optimistic about our long-term future prospects. Our access to the United States market, even though it is largely restricted to the export of raw materials and semi-processed goods, is the envy, as Prime Minister Menzies said, of most nations in the world.
We should remember that the considerable volume of Canadian exports to the United States is one of the great strengths in the Canadian economy and an important reason for our optimism about the long-term future. It seems to me that we should do nothing that would disturb this. That objective is not inconsistent with the broad intentions apparently in the minds of those who are charged with responsibility at the present time in the United Kingdom.
The Prime Minister is one of those who strongly supported my colleague, the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), in his efforts to incorporate into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization article II, by which we sought to supplement military cooperation by economic co-operation among those countries who were the original signatories to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization itself. It seems to me that the policy of the government revealed by its

The Address-Hon. Paul Martin negative attitude to the British proposal, by the reckless manner in which it has made its own proposals, indicates that the government is not acting in a manner consistent with the declared purposes of the Prime Minister several years ago as to the great value of economic as well as political co-operation among the free nations of the world who are members of the defensive alliance which was established as the result of an effort to try to resist aggression from any quarter.
If my hon. friends are sincere about commonwealth trade why did the Prime Minister of this country, when Mr. Macmillan came to Ottawa, not take advantage of that opportunity at least to outline to him for the first time the nature of his own proposal for a 15 per cent shift? I asked the Prime Minister on Friday, the day Prime Minister Macmillian arrived, whether he would take advantage of Mr. Macmillan's presence in Ottawa over Friday night and Saturday to discuss further the details about the United Kingdom proposal for free trade and his own proposal for a 15 per cent shift. This was the reply of the man who speaks feverishly and sometimes almost with excessive emotion about what he is going to do for the commonwealth: "I will if there is time."
On the Monday after this visit, when the Prime Minister had conferred with the British prime minister, discussing, I know, very important matters which arose out of the discussions between the President of the United States and the prime minister of Great Britain, I asked the Prime Minister if he had taken advantage of the opportunity of the visit in Ottawa of the British prime minister to discuss with the latter his important proposal of a 15 per cent shift and the proposal put forward by Her Majesty's chancellor of the exchequer for a free trade area between Canada and the United Kingdom. This Prime Minister who, as I say, regards himself as a champion of commonwealth unity and is regarded as such now by a great section of the press in the United Kingdom, made the categorical answer to me: no.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we have to accept the observations made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) that there are reasons for believing that political considerations had something to do with the claims made by hon. gentlemen opposite during the election campaign and with the statements they are now making about ways and means of improving our trade position with the United Kingdom and with other commonwealth countries. Let no one say that from my remarks it can be construed that we are not desirous of seeing trade promoted between this country and other common-
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).l
wealth countries. We recognize the need for a political community of interest and in this very difficult period we must acknowledge the need for an economic community of interest. But it is one thing to make a boast of intention and it is something else to give proper indication as to how that intention best can be fulfilled. I submit that, good as it may be and enjoyable as I am sure it will be, the delegation of 50 Canadian businessmen headed by my genial friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not going to bring about a revolution in the trade between the United Kingdom and this country.
By the way, in passing I should like to inquire why the automobile industry, one of the important sections of the industrial life of this community, is not represented in that delegation. The minister may have a good reason and I hope that at some time before he leaves for the United Kingdom he will tell us about this. But the house will recall that I asked him on several occasions whether he was going to the United Kingdom with this delegation and, if he went, whether he would discuss trade matters with his opposite numbers. While I do not remember the exact words he used, Hansard will bear me out when I say that his reply was to this effect, "Well, that would depend upon instructions I receive from my Prime Minister". Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons why this government is floundering is that it is a do-it-yourself government. It is a government made up of a group of well-meaning individuals headed by a Prime Minister whose confidence in himself is such that he believes that he alone can make government pronouncements and that he alone can bring this nation back to economic safety and normalcy.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I listened the other day with equal interest to a speech of the same length delivered by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson). I take it that the speech in each case was at least to some extent a pitch or a bid for the leadership of the Liberal party at their coming national convention. I am sure that anyone who heard both speeches, and who knew nothing else about the two hon. gentlemen, would have the greatest difficulty in deciding which one to support. Anyone listening to those two speeches would have even greater difficulty I am sure, in attempting to ascertain the trade policy if any, of the Liberal party at this time. Both speeches dealt with trade. We heard from them for a total of 80 minutes. While they suggested that the government's trade policy was not what it should be and that the government at times had made statements that were rather reckless and inopportune, one certainly could not criticize them for having stuck their necks out or for having provided any leadership in the way of suggesting a trade policy.
Another thing which I think was notably absent from the speech of the hon. member for Essex East was any reference to the speech made this morning and the amendment moved by his colleague the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix). Speaking as he did as a prominent member of his party following the the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment this morning, I would have thought that he might have placed on the record the official position, if there is one, of the Liberal party on this extremely important amendment. As far as we in this group are concerned, over the years we have always supported the idea and the principle that the time would arrive when Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag. When we first supported that idea as a political party I am sure that it did not have the same general support across this country as it
The Address-Mr. Argue now has. It would seem that in 1957 the people of this nation, in a spirit of great unity, have come to support the idea of a distinctive and truly Canadian flag.
Many speeches have been made on this subject in the past. I think it is fair to say that all political parties have given support to this idea in one form or another. The former leader of the opposition Hon. George Drew in 1953 I believe made a very eloquent speech supporting the principle of a distinctive Canadian flag. We know that as far back as 1946 a special committee of this house did a great deal of work on this subject and made a report-I think it was almost unanimous- supporting a distinctive Canadian flag and contributing a suggestion for such a flag. I am not going to say at this time-indeed I am not sure-what type of design I would support myself, whether it be the exact design presented by that parliamentary committee or some other design. However, it seems to me that at this session of parliament we should be able to give some consideration to making a step forward towards the day that we have in this country a distinctive Canadian flag.
Towards the end of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I expect to move an amendment to the present amendment that is before the house. I am not quarrelling with the principle of the amendment but there is one part of it, as it now stands, which I think could be changed. The present amendment reads as follows:
We respectfully urge, however, that Canada should have a distinctive national flag and, in the opinion of this house, your most gracious Majesty's advisers should consider at once the advisability of taking steps to give to this country a truly Canadian flag.
We suggest that this amendment is asking the government itself to take these steps to provide a truly Canadian flag. We do not feel that this should be the prerogative of the government to decide precisely how it might best adopt for this nation a truly Canadian flag.
We feel that the question of arriving at a flag of a distinctive nature for Canada is something that is not a government measure but is something which should be reached by the agreement of all the major political parties in this house. We suggest that the government itself should not be making the decision but should be providing the means by which parliament, representative as it is of the Canadian nation, can make the decision. The amendment I shall move at a later time is as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "taking steps" and by substituting therefor the following words:

"to make it possible for parliament to reach an early decision with respect to a truly Canadian flag."
I would ask that the government and the house leader give consideration to this suggestion: that the form of this motion with a subamendment added thereto should not be taken in the spirit of being a want of confidence motion. The government should not consider that its own life as a government should be at stake in the vote on this resolution.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made last night by the Minister of Finance and in many respects in the things he said he blew rather hot at times and rather cold at others. One thing he did not seem to be able to make up his mind about was whether the government had sufficient confidence of this house, whether it had too much or too little confidence. In his remarks he chastised a member of the official opposition for being so anxious to get up and support the government with might and main. Towards the end of his speech he said "Give us the confidence and we will do the job".
That last reference looked to me like an admission, in view of the things he had to say in the opening part of his speech, that the government was terrified most of all of this one thing: that in the various votes the government might keep the confidence of the house and therefore have to deal now with the great national issues which face this country because, as I see the things the government has done so far, and they have been good in the main, they have not dealt with the root of the basic problems which face our country.
I agree with those who have said that within the period of eight weeks or, if you wish to take the full term of office of this

government within the period of five months, more has been accomplished than in any similar period for some years in the history of Canada. I say the fact that something more has been accomplished is an indication that the present position, where the government has a minority in this house, is the best goad there is for government action and the best assurance to the public of this nation that democracy is functioning in our country. I think when the vote is taken on the subamendment to which I have referred we shall then see to what extent this government believes in full democracy in parliament because I do not think it is necessarily the best thing that these great national issues should be decided by one party in the traditional sense that the Prime Minister makes up his mind, then there is cabinet solidarity and therefore party solidarity and, no matter what the issue, something is rammed through parliament which in many instances people do not like.
I remember last year as a member of a standing committee on agriculture, taking part in the great debate on payments for sheep-as to whether it was overpaid or not. I also remember sitting on many committees in this house where a pattern has been followed and if there was a controversial issue referred to the committee, that committee was used by a government with a majority of the members of the committee to stifle discussion and to prevent full consideration of the report. We suspected in many instances the reports were written not really by the committee but initially in the office of the minister of the department concerned, and the report was then handed to the members of the government party, that is to say the Liberal party, and the great "whitewash" took place.

I can appreciate that there may be exceptions, and if something different was done in that case, it was the exception which proves the rule, because I have sat in so many of these committee meetings-committees of which the former minister has been a member, or whose proceedings he has watched from the bleachers because he was very much affected by the discussions-when a rubber-stamp report was made, a report which was not supported by anybody except members of the government.
The Address-Mr. Argue
Mr. Speaker, measures have been passed this session providing for cash advances, increases in old age pensions, blind persons' pensions, disability pensions, war veterans' allowances and so on; they have all been passed through their various stages. It would seem to me that people in the country generally feel that something is being accomplished in the present session of parliament, and accomplished with reasonable despatch; and they will not look kindly on a government which wants to duck some of the most important issues which face the country, and escape them, possibly by calling an election which, according to this morning's press, would cost almost $7 million on the basis of the cost of the last election.
We have heard a good deal from the Minister of Finance both in the course of his speech last night and through the answers he has given to questions asked in the house, and one of the questions most often asked of the minister was whether there would be a budget. I suspect now that there will be no budget introduced this session. I have heard many speeches by many ministers of finance in the past, but I have never heard a speech which was quite so reckless and irresponsible or so verbose as the speech delivered last night by the present minister.
I think that speech contained many statements which cannot be substantiated on a basis of fact. The minister made a statement which I felt was rather reckless when he said the threat on inflation in Canada had now been checked. He took that position because the cost of living index has appeared to level off to some extent, although it is still going up. To my mind, the figures provide no such indication; rather, they are an indication of a further loss of revenue to primary producers and a further reflection of the deterioration of the position of agricultural producers in this country. The daily bulletin put out by the dominion bureau of statistics relating to this increase in the cost of living from 123.3 to 123.4 had this to say:
In the current month a decline in the food index from 121.9 to 121.7 was not quite sufficient to balance increases in the other four component groups. Substantially lower prices were reported for pork, with lesser declines for beef, most fresh and canned fruits and vegetables, margarine, coffee and eggs.
There it is, the check to inflation which the Minister of Finance was talking about last night. Any check there is has been brought about mainly because the prices of pork, beef, fresh and canned fruits, vegetables and eggs have fallen. I do not think that is a situation with regard to which the government should feel much satisfaction. With

The Address-Mr. Argue regard to this suggested arrest of the inflationary spiral, we in this group have been asking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) what he intends to do about setting an adequate floor price for hogs. Mr. Speaker, if one was sitting in this house and did not know what changes had taken place, and was relying merely on the answers given by the present Minister of Agriculture and by his predecessor in office there would be no means of telling which one of them was replying.
Somebody in the Department of Agriculture is evidently good at statistics. If they cannot go back one year to prove things are not so bad, they go back two years or ten years or twenty years. Thus we have the spectacle of the Minister of Agriculture getting up and saying: do not blame us for what has happened since we took office, just relate the situation today to what it was a year ago. Even on that basis there is not too much for the government to be satisfied with, because the price of cattle has been softening. Our complaint about the price of hogs is that almost ever since this government took office this price has been dropping at a very rapid rate.
On June 22 this year, the day after the government took office, the price of hogs at Toronto, grade B-l dressed, was $31.50. For the week ending November 2, 1957 the price was down to $26.25, a drop of more than $5 a hundred. The price a year ago was not much different, but the price in the same period a year ago had increased from $27.50 on June 22 to $29.50 in November. That is what happened in the period of the summer and fall months last year. Hog prices stayed relatively stable in this country. What has happened since June 21? Hog prices have been fluctuating, but the trend has been downward; there has been a very substantial drop, and one hopes that in these circumstances the government will come forward with proposals to place an adequate floor price on hogs, and that it will not stand up, as its representatives have done in this house, and say: the old floor price has not yet been reached, so what are you complaining about? If all this government can do by way of price support legislation is to repeat the type of legislation which the former administration placed on the statute books, I think their support in rural Canada will not be any greater than it was during the time of the former administration.
The case of oats and barley provides another instance in which prices paid for agricultural products have fallen. The sale price of these products today is very little


higher than the initial price, two cents a bushel in the case of No. 1 feed barley and about seven cents in the case of No. 1 feed oats. This means that at this moment the Canadian wheat board in its oats and barley operation is almost certainly suffering a net loss. That in turn will mean no further interim payments, no further final payment and, in fact, it represents such a low selling price as will require moneys to be paid into the wheat board account from the national treasury. Is this the way to check inflation? I think the truth of the matter is that the threat of inflation has not been checked.
I note that an application was before the board of transport commissioners some weeks ago asking for a further 10 per cent increase in freight rates in this country. Would the Minister of Finance or any member of the government say that there would not be an increase in freight rates? Does the government suggest that a substantial increase in freight rates is not an inflationary move? I think it is. There have been recent increases in prices of farm machinery and automobiles; are these increases not considered inflationary? I think the very announcement made by the Minister of Finance last night to the effect that the bank rediscount rate and interest rates generally would probably soften and that we are going to move away from the tight money policy of the former administration is in itself an indication that inflation has not been checked. I think the Minister of Finance will have to withdraw that statement as the months go by because, as we see it, inflation is certain to continue under the policies of this administration.
The Minister of Finance is satisfied that he has dealt with inflation. He is satisfied also that the government has dealt with the trade problem in spite of the two speeches to which I have referred. Indeed, he seems satisfied that everything is being done to increase markets for Canadian products. Moreover, he seems most satisfied that everything that conceivably could be done to increase our export markets for grain has been done. On November 14, as reported at page 1162 of Hansard of that date, the Minister of Finance said:
-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has thrown into sound disposal policies with respect to that wheat an energy which has not been exhibited in that respect for many and many a year.
A little later he went on to say:
-in the matter of our trade undertakings we have fulfilled our undertakings to the letter.
I thought one undertaking of this government was to recover the overseas markets for agricultural products that had been lost.

The Minister of Finance tells us the government has accomplished its undertakings, yet we see a substantial fall in exports for Canadian agricultural products since this government took office.
I am now going to compare the exports of wheat in July of this year as compared with July of last year, July being the first full month in which this government was in office. Wheat exports dropped from 28 million bushels in July 1956 to 22i million bushels in July 1957, a decrease of 5J million bushels. In August this year our exports of wheat dropped by 3 million bushels compared to last year. There was a further drop of 3J million bushels in September this year as compared to the same month a year ago. The figures covering our barley exports for the same period indicate that there was a drop of 2 million bushels in July 1957 as compared to last year, a drop of 6 million bushels in August and a drop of 3 million bushels in September compared to the figures for the same months a year ago.
The government has been in office since June-not long it is true; not long in which to redirect new export policies-but the Minister of Finance stands up in the house and says that the undertakings of the government have been accomplished as far as international trade is concerned, and with the accomplishment of the undertakings of the government referred to by the minister we have witnessed an extremely drastic drop in export markets for wheat and barley. Is that the satisfactory situation for which the government now wishes to claim so much credit? As far as inflation and trade are concerned I think the government has a long way to go to solve these pressing problems.
There is something else which the government has not yet tackled. We heard from members over the years when they were in opposition the constant cry that there should be set up a committee of this house to examine into the question of defence expenditures but now that the situation is reversed the new government does not seem anxious to have such a committee established. We are all aware of the new state of defence in the world and the new potential threat created by the existence of sputniks. I think every hon. member of this house fully supports international co-operation amongst friendly nations for the maximum amount of defence that can be provided for the free nations and I think we all support the NATO provisions for defence. I think one can judge from what one reads in the press, that the NATO shield, as it is being called, and the NATO forces are sufficient, if war occurred, to wipe out the soviet union, as a military force, yes almost as a nation. I do not think there is any one in this house who
The Address-Mr. Argue believes that if such a war came we would not be wiped out too; so where do we go from here when each camp apparently has weapons of a type and in such quantity as to completely destroy its possible opponent?
The battle for men's minds still continues. It is still most important that we do everything we can in a practical way to ensure the maintenance of freedom throughout the world in those countries that enjoy political freedom and work to extend it; but I think the time has long since passed when we can say to ourselves that an expenditure of almost $2 billion on our current type of national defence provides real defence. A man of such prominence as Lieutenant-General Guy Simonds, the former chief of the general staff, has said that 80 per cent of our defence forces are obsolete. He said that the $200 million or $300 million that has been spent on the development of the CF-105 has been wasted, that the CF-105 is now a dead duck. What is this government doing? It says it is going to continue its development. When we asked to find out by way of a parliamentary committee whether a statement by a person of the prominence of Lieutenant-General Simonds is correct or not the government would not provide us with such a committee. We had hoped that this government would see the folly in putting all of our defence projects, or almost all of such eggs, in a military basket.
I had hoped the government would see the immediate necessity of making substantial increases in economic assistance to friendly nations, expanding the assistance given by Canada under the Colombo plan, not in a small meagre or mediocre way but under a great plan whereby Canada could lead the world in relation to its resources in the provision of economic and technical assistance to people in free nations. The government increased Canada's contribution under the Colombo plan; indeed the announcement was made the other day. It is no longer going to make the small contribution of $34,400,000; rather it is increasing its contribution to $35 million, less than a 2 per cent increase. The Colombo plan is designed to help lend economic assistance and technical development to the commonwealth countries and southeast Asia and I suggest it is there where the future course of democracy in the world will be decided in terms of whether it increases in strength or decreases.
My study of the program of the Nehru government suggests to me that India today is in a deep financial crisis. Earl Atlee, according to this morning's press, said that India has decided to use almost all of its sterling reserves in meeting the great economic crisis which faces that country. Are we going to do something now in a spectacular, dynamic

The Address-Mr. Green way to show the world that we mean business in economic assistance and in helping our fellow men?
The idea that I am about to present is not new; I presented it in the house on April 13, 1954. I said at that time I felt that the time had arrived when we should take $500 million out of our defence budget, being spent on armaments, and use it for economic assistance.
I believe my time is about up, Mr. Speaker. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "taking steps" and by substituting therefor the following words:
"to make it possible for parliament to reach an early decision with respect to a truly Canadian flag".
I would go further, Mr. Speaker, and say that the Canadian people are prepared to provide economic assistance to underdeveloped countries not just by transferring the amount of money they have in a defence program now to some other program, but I believe the Canadian people are willing to pay the price and to pay the cost of providing our share of the economic assistance that may be necessary to see that friendly nations are able to maintain democracy in their countries.
I have been informed that recently the British labour party announced that if they are returned to power in the next election they would be prepared to take three per cent of the gross national product of Great Britain and use it for economic assistance to underdeveloped nations. I suggest that Canada should do the same thing; that $1 billion as a long-term investment program from Canada in a planned way is not too much to suggest as our share of the price that must be paid to see that democracy is retained in those parts of the world that now enjoy it.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon it is my privilege to say a few words on behalf of the government in closing this throne speech debate. In the first place, may I say that we appreciate the suggestions and the criticisms-although they are a little harder to appreciate,-which have come our way in the course of this debate. After all, in a debate of this kind we have the democratic system at its best, and the debate has been an excellent one. We are particularly proud of the part which has been taken by the new members of our own party of whom we elected so many. We are fortunate in having, I think, a larger proportion of new members in the present house than any government has


had for some time. Without exception these young men have shown-I am sure everyone in the house will admit this-that they are deeply and genuinely interested in the welfare of the country and are not hesitant about making suggestions to their own ministers. That, of course, is as it should be.
We have before us at the moment an amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) which would add to the address the following words:
We respectfully urge, however, that Canada should have a distinctive national flag and, in the opinion of this house, your most gracious Majesty's advisers should consider at once the advisability of taking steps to give to this country a truly Canadian flag.
To that amendment the hon. member for Assiniboia has moved a subamendment this afternoon which deletes the words:
to give to this country a truly Canadian flagand substitutes:
to make it possible for parliament to reach an early decision with respect to a truly Canadian flag.
In moving this subamendment the hon. member directed some honeyed words to the government. He said: After all, this may be a vote of no confidence but, nevertheless, let us not treat it as such; let us just be on a friendly basis and forget all about this being a vote of no confidence. Well, he is a very experienced politician. He has been here for a long time and he knows just as well as I do, and as all the other members of the house do, that this amendment and the subamendment which have been moved today, if they were approved by the house would constitute a vote of no confidence, and for that reason they cannot be accepted by the government.
I agree that this flag question is a very important one; but I point out that the manner in which the issue has been brought before the house today is really ridiculous, It should never have been tossed into a debate of this kind. Other steps might have been taken by way of a motion, or something of that kind, so that the question could have been considered in the manner which it merits. It does merit the most careful consideration and that is absolutely impossible under the conditions in which this amendment has been moved today.
I should like to say a few words about the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). He is a great admirer of minority government and why would he not be? Where the government of the country does not have a majority the members of his party believe that that gives them a chance to hold a gun at the head of the

government and say, "Here, you do what we want or we will pull the trigger". Now, this is just a splendid illustration of the futility of a four-party system in a democratic country. Our whole system of government is based on the government of the day having the responsibility of giving leadership to the Canadian people.

speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend, who is in such a delightfully happy and friendly mood today, could give us the agenda of the proposed commonwealth conference which is to be held?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, did you ever hear a more foolish question? Now I know he will never win that leadership. This economic and trade conference is to take place next year. I suggest to these Jeremiahs across the way that they forget trying to wish it into failure and that they do what they can to make it a great success. If they believe in promoting commonwealth trade half as much as the hon. member for Essex East tried to tell us today, I am sure they will all accept my suggestion.
Then he complained at considerable length about an attempt being made to shift Canada's purchases from the United States. He tried to strengthen his argument on that point by dealing with exports from Canada to the United States and in so doing I thought he was drawing a rather long bow. The actual fact is-and the hon. member for Essex East knows it very well-that last year the adverse trade balance against Canada in her trade with the United States was over $1,200 million or over $100 million a month. But the Liberal government, before the election, was not a bit interested in that matter. Right Hon. C. D. Howe said it was a good thing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: So it was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Canadian people decided that question, just as they decided several other questions, on June 10. I am really amazed that the hon. member for Essex East would rise in his place today and make a speech in which he criticized the present government for trying to get that adverse trade balance reduced. It is things of this sort that make one place little value on his remarks.

speechtext:
After all, the main subject for debate should be the speech from the throne. I am going to presume on the good nature of the house by reading again just one paragraph from an article written for the Vancouver Sun by our old friend Elmore Philpott who sat here during the last parliament and who is now with us in the press gallery. Mr. Philpott never made any attempt to hide the fact that he is an ardent Liberal. In this report written to his paper after the commencement of the present session, he had this to say under the heading "Keeping Faith":
Ottawa-The 1957 speech from the throne is an historic document for several reasons. But the one which means most to the people of Canada is that the Conservatives have spectacularly kept their main election promises.
And may I say that every word of this is true.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The article continues:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has not only itemized the main points on which he was morally bound to take action at this session, but he has also outlined intended action on several other matters which he might well have postponed for the future without giving justification for the cry of bad faith.
The whole country, regardless of party preference, should be delighted to see this proof that the old party of Sir John A. Macdonald has thus demonstrated that its official title of "Progressive Conservatives'' has taken on new meaning for the whole Canadian nation.
How could the present government have a finer endorsation than the one I have just read?
I need only remind hon. members that the house has already enacted legislation to provide for cash advances on farm-stored grain, has already increased the payments under the Old Age Security Act, has made possible increased payments under the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act an the Disabled Persons Act, and has increased the benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act. These are all bills which have already been passed by this house, and some of them have received royal assent.
Other measures on the order paper are the bill to provide annual vacations with pay for employees in federal works, undertakings and businesses; a bill to amend the Pension Act which has already passed the resolution stage; a resolution preceding a measure to establish a system of guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities; and a resolution that it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the construction of a branch line for the Canadian National Railways. These are measures actually passed or in the process of being passed by this

The Address-Mr. Green house, in most cases implementing the campaign promises made by the Conservative party.
Yesterday announcement was made of a policy which will implement the paragraph in the speech from the throne dealing with power in the Atlantic provinces.
We have acted in other fields as well.
When we came into office we found that as a result of deliberate policy pursued by the former government the construction of homes in Canada had dropped off to an alarming degree. That was a tragedy, not only for the young people and other Canadians who needed homes of their own or needed homes to rent but for the building industry of Canada and other connected industries such as the suppliers of furniture and all the articles that go with the building of a home. In that particular field, when we took over, there was rapidly developing a spirit of defeatism which might very well have cast a great shadow over the national economy in the months that lay ahead. Fortunately it was not necessary for us to have legislation in order to do something to meet that situation and we decided that $150 million should be made available for the construction of lower priced homes in Canada. That was being done by means of what are known as agency loans where the government puts up the money and the loans are made through the banks and other lending institutions.
We were not absolutely sure that such a plan would be successful but we have been very gratified by the results. I have before me the figures up to November 8 last, which was only nine weeks after the plan really came into effect, and at that time loans had been approved to the amount of $93,309,331 for a total number of units of 9,995. In addition to those loans which had been approved there were in process of approval loans amounting to another $35,710,000 making a total of $129,019,331. That means that the money is rapidly being used up and I may say that if there is a need for an additional amount under the scheme the government will be taking steps to meet that situation. There has been some holding back and there have been some difficulties with respect to the Atlantic provinces. In that area, as of the end of last week, there had been only 201 units covered by loan but that figure did not include applications which had not yet been approved. The money committed to these loans in the Atlantic provinces totalled $1,712,232.66. There had also been some delay in the province of British Columbia, but in that province the situation is much better than formerly and the figures for British

Columbia as of the end of last week were 466 units for a total value of $3,988,089.11.

I think we have already shown we are endeavouring to give leadership to the Canadian people and I believe the Canadian people are fair enough and reasonable enough to realize that fact, no matter how much abuse we might get from the other side of the house.

members of the former cabinet had to do- and the same applies to members of this cabinet if they wish to follow the practice- was to get up and read something on a sheet of paper. This practice was followed quite frequently by former ministers and, in fact, we had quite a bit of it from the hon. member for Essex East this afternoon, but no doubt he got into that bad habit while he was a member of the government.
I should like to say this before I close: We have had the finest assistance from the members of the Canadian civil service. I know the former ministers will agree with these comments. These men and women are in the civil service as a career; it is their life. They have been supported for many years now by leaders of all the parties; all the leaders of all the parties since Sir Robert Borden introduced the merit system about the time of the first world war. They have stood firmly behind that system. Today Canada has reaped her
The Address-Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent reward from that policy. Here we had these senior civil servants-I do not suppose one of them had ever been in a senior position except under a Liberal minister-and yet these men and women have served us devotedly. They really have rendered a great service for Canada. I hope-I am sure-that it will always be possible for Canada to keep a civil service of that type.
Mr. Speaker, the time has practically gone and we must vote on these amendments. I repeat once again, for the benefit of those who were not here when I began my remarks, that this amendment and the subamendment would, if endorsed, mean that this house is voting no confidence in the present government. No matter what attempt may be made to picture them as something else, that is what they actually are. If one of them were to be adopted by this house, that vote would constitute a vote of non-confidence in the present administration.

Mr. Speaker, I think there are still two minutes before the time at which you will be required by the rules of the house to put the question. We have heard a speech, very amusing in parts, from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), but there are realities which we have to face and which, I am sure, he and his colleagues are prepared to continue to face as a result of June 10.
The hon. gentleman has said that it is not very comfortable to be a member of a government which does not have a majority in the House of Commons. But that is the situation which arose as a consequence of the election of June 10, and it was under those conditions that the former government resigned and the hon. gentleman's leader accepted the responsibility of forming a cabinet. It is that situation which we have faced since parliament met on October 14.
We declared that we would not obstruct the government in its efforts to implement the promises it had made during the election campaign, and I declared in my first remarks on the address in reply to the speech from the throne that it was not our intention this session to move an amendment to the motion for an address, and that having come to that conclusion it was not our intention to support amendments made from any other quarter of the house, because there could be only one of two consequences; if the amendment carried the government would be defeated and would be prevented from putting before parliament the legislation

We will, following their rejection, as I expect they will be rejected, not oppose the main motion to express thanks to our gracious sovereign for having opened this session of parliament. 6.	Assisted passage.
The purpose of the assisted passage loan scheme is to assist suitable immigrants in financing the cost of their transportation to Canada. The loans are interest-free and are available to cover the cost of transportation for dependants as well as for the working

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: head of the family in cases where this financial assistance is necessary, and also to residents of Canada who are anxious to bring their dependants, i.e. wives and unmarried minor children, to this country but do not have sufficient funds to cover the passage cost. Residents of Canada may apply at the nearest immigration office. Application may be made overseas at the Canadian immigration office in the country of the prospective immigrant's residence. Assisted passage loans are issued in the form of a transportation warrant Imm. 500 which are exchanged by the transportation company for steamship or air passage tickets which include inland transportation. The transportation company forwards to the chief treasury officer an invoice accompanied by the original Imm. 500 and is reimbursed by the chief treasury officer.
